mac.verdict.panic_title: one: Your Mac had a kernel panic | other: Your Mac had {0} kernel panics
mac.verdict.panic_body: A kernel panic is the Mac equivalent of a blue screen: macOS stopped to protect your data, then restarted. Open the crash for the details.
mac.verdict.panic_kext: The extension {0} appears in the crash: it is the most likely cause. Update or uninstall the software that installed it.
mac.verdict.restart_body: The last restart was not a normal shutdown (system watchdog or a long press on the power button). If the Mac froze, note what was connected and open at the time.
mac.verdict.memory_title: macOS often runs out of memory
mac.verdict.memory_body: macOS had to close apps several times to free memory. Check the Memory tab of Activity Monitor and keep at least 10 % of the disk free.
mac.verdict.stable_body: No kernel panic or unexpected restart in the last 30 days.

mac.check.panic_detail: one: The Mac restarted after a kernel panic in the last {2} days (last: {1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm}). | other: The Mac restarted after {0} kernel panics in the last {2} days (last: {1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm}).
mac.check.panic_advice_kext: Update or uninstall the software that installed {0}: it is the most likely cause.
mac.check.panic_advice_generic: Update macOS and your apps. If it happens again, note what you were doing and contact Apple support.
mac.check.restart_title: The last restart was not a normal shutdown
mac.check.restart_detail:
Started {0:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm}. Recorded cause: {1}.
Raw value: {2}
mac.check.restart_advice: If the Mac froze and you held the power button, this is expected. If it restarted by itself, watch for repeats and check the accessories connected at the time. (Apple does not document these codes: the reading is approximate.)
mac.check.app_crashed: one: {1} crashed once | other: {1} crashed {0} times
mac.check.app_apple_advice: This is an Apple background process: it is usually harmless unless you notice a problem. Updating macOS often fixes it.
mac.check.app_advice: Update the app. If it keeps crashing, reset its preferences or reinstall it.
mac.check.jetsam_title: one: macOS ran low on memory once | other: macOS ran low on memory {0} times
mac.check.jetsam_detail: one: macOS closed processes to free memory (one "Jetsam" report in {1} days). | other: macOS closed processes to free memory ({0} "Jetsam" reports in {1} days).
mac.check.jetsam_advice: Look at the Memory tab of Activity Monitor around those times: browsers with many tabs, virtual machines and creative apps use the most. Low free disk space makes it worse (less room for swap).
mac.check.kext_loaded_detail: Version {0}{1}. Kernel extensions run inside the macOS kernel; on Apple Silicon they need reduced security in Startup Security Utility.
mac.check.kext_loaded_advice: Check that it is still needed and up to date. Most vendors now provide a system extension or a DriverKit driver instead.
mac.check.kext_leftover_title: Kernel extension installed but not loaded: {0}
mac.check.kext_leftover_detail: {0}{1}. Often left behind by uninstalled software.
mac.check.kext_leftover_advice: If you no longer use this software, remove it with its vendor's uninstaller.
mac.check.sysext_title: one: One system extension installed | other: {0} system extensions installed
mac.check.sysext_advice: Security, VPN and network-filter extensions can slow down or block the network. Turn off the ones you do not use in System Settings › General › Login Items & Extensions.
mac.check.smart_advice: Back up now. An internal drive in this state needs Apple support.
mac.check.disk_title: Low free space on the startup disk ({0:0.#} %)
mac.check.disk_detail: {0:0.#} GB free out of {1:0.#} GB. macOS needs room for swap, updates and caches.
mac.check.disk_advice: Free up space in System Settings › General › Storage. Keep at least 10 % free.
mac.check.battery_advice: A worn battery can cause sudden shutdowns under load. Apple recommends a battery service below 80 %.
mac.check.cycles_title: Battery past its rated cycle count
mac.check.cycles_advice: Plan a battery service if battery life drops.
mac.check.os_detail: Apple fixes security issues in the current macOS and the two previous ones.
mac.check.os_advice: Update macOS if your Mac supports a newer version.
mac.check.sip_detail: SIP protects system files from changes, including by kernel extensions.
mac.check.sip_advice: Turn it back on from recoveryOS (csrutil enable) unless you need it off.
mac.check.gk_detail: Apps are no longer checked for a valid signature when they open.
mac.check.gk_advice: Turn it back on in Terminal: sudo spctl --master-enable.
mac.check.uptime_title: one: No restart for {0} day | other: No restart for {0} days
mac.check.uptime_detail: Some updates and memory fixes apply only after a restart.
mac.check.ok_detail: No kernel panic, repeated crash or hardware warning in the last {0} days.
mac.panic_explain.watchdog: A core system process stopped responding for several minutes, so macOS restarted the kernel. The process is named after "no successful checkins from" in the report.
mac.panic_advice.watchdog: If it is WindowServer, suspect graphics: external displays, docks and adapters, screen recording or window-management apps. Unplug accessories and update or remove such apps.
mac.panic_explain.sleep_wake: The Mac failed to go to sleep or wake up in time.
mac.panic_advice.sleep_wake: Disconnect USB / Thunderbolt accessories and docks before sleep, then test again. Apps that keep devices busy (backup, sync, VPN) can block sleep.
mac.panic_explain.gpu: The panic was raised by the graphics driver.
mac.panic_advice.gpu: Update macOS, then test without external displays and without GPU-heavy apps (games, 3D, video export). If it happens again on a clean system, contact Apple support.
mac.panic_explain.storage: The panic involves the SSD controller.
mac.panic_advice.storage: Check free space (keep at least 10 %), back up now and run First Aid in Disk Utility. Repeated storage panics on Apple Silicon need Apple support.
mac.panic_explain.kernel_memory: The kernel ran out of memory for its own structures, usually because a kernel or system extension leaks memory.
mac.panic_advice.kernel_memory: Look at third-party kernel and system extensions (security, VPN, file systems) and update or remove them.
mac.panic_explain.thunderbolt_usb: The panic involves the USB or Thunderbolt stack.
mac.panic_advice.thunderbolt_usb: Test without docks, hubs and adapters, then reconnect them one at a time. Update the dock firmware if the vendor offers one.
mac.panic_explain.data_abort: Kernel code read or ran from an invalid address. This is usually a bug in a kernel extension, more rarely a hardware fault.
mac.panic_advice.data_abort: If a non-Apple extension appears in the backtrace, update or uninstall it. Otherwise update macOS and watch for repeats.
mac.panic_explain.thermal: The panic mentions a thermal event.
mac.panic_advice.thermal: Keep the vents clear, use the Mac on a hard surface and check which apps load the CPU or GPU in Activity Monitor.
mac.shutdown.wdog: a hardware watchdog reset (the system had stopped responding)
mac.shutdown.btn_rst: a forced restart with the power button (long press)
mac.shutdown.crash: a crash was recorded before the restart
mac.plain.panic: macOS hit an error it could not recover from in its core (the kernel), stopped everything to protect your data and restarted. It is the Mac equivalent of a blue screen.
mac.plain.panic_kext: The non-Apple extension {0} was running at that moment: it is the first suspect.
mac.plain.restart: The Mac did not shut down normally: the system had stopped responding (watchdog) or the power button was held. No panic report was written, so the exact cause is unknown.
mac.plain.jetsam: Memory was full, so macOS closed apps or background processes to keep the system responsive. Open apps may have quit or reloaded.
mac.plain.exc.sigterm_timeout: macOS asked the process to quit (logout, update or end of a task) and it did not stop in time, so macOS forced it. This is usually harmless.
mac.plain.exc.bad_access: The app tried to use memory it had no right to. It is a bug in the app or one of its plug-ins, sometimes triggered by a corrupted cache or file.
mac.plain.exc.abort: The app detected an internal error and stopped itself on purpose.
mac.plain.exc.kill: macOS ended the app on purpose: it stopped responding, used too many resources or did not quit when asked.
mac.plain.exc.breakpoint: An internal safety check of the app failed (a programming error), so it stopped.
mac.plain.exc.bad_instruction: The app ran an invalid instruction: usually a bug, sometimes an app built for another processor.
mac.plain.exc.resource: The app went past a limit set by macOS (memory, processor time or disk writes) and was stopped.
mac.plain.exc.guard: The app misused a resource that macOS protects (for example a file or a port).
mac.plain.exc.other: The app stopped unexpectedly. The details below say how; updating or reinstalling the app usually helps.
mac.evidence.kext: {0} is blamed because it is the first non-Apple extension in the panic backtrace.
mac.toast.file_not_report: This file is not a crash report Dump Finder can read.

mac.kb.watchdog.title: The Mac freezes, then restarts with a "watchdog" panic
mac.kb.watchdog.symptoms: The screen freezes for a minute or more, the pointer may still move, then the Mac restarts. The report says "userspace watchdog timeout", often naming WindowServer.
mac.kb.watchdog.cause: A core process stopped answering macOS. When it is WindowServer (the process that draws the screen), external displays, docks, display adapters, screen-recording and window-management apps are the usual suspects.
mac.kb.watchdog.fix: Update macOS. Unplug docks and adapters and test with displays connected directly. Quit or update screen-recording, window-management and display-tuning apps, then add them back one by one.
mac.kb.sleep_wake.title: Panic or restart when the Mac sleeps or wakes
mac.kb.sleep_wake.symptoms: The Mac is found restarted in the morning, or will not wake from sleep. The report mentions sleep, wake or a timed-out transition.
mac.kb.sleep_wake.cause: An accessory or a driver did not answer during the sleep transition. Docks, USB hubs, audio interfaces and apps that keep devices busy (backup, sync, VPN) are frequent causes.
mac.kb.sleep_wake.fix: Unplug accessories before sleep for a few days to confirm. Update the dock firmware and the apps that use the accessories. Check System Settings › Battery › Options (or Energy) for settings that keep the Mac awake.
mac.kb.kexts.title: Kernel panics caused by third-party kernel extensions
mac.kb.kexts.symptoms: Repeated panics whose report lists a non-Apple bundle id (com.vendor…) under "Kernel Extensions in backtrace".
mac.kb.kexts.cause: Kernel extensions run inside the kernel: a bug in them crashes the whole Mac. On Apple Silicon they need reduced security; antivirus, VPN, NTFS file-system drivers, virtualization and old audio drivers still use them.
mac.kb.kexts.fix: Update the software that installed the extension, or uninstall it with the vendor's uninstaller. Prefer versions that use a system extension or DriverKit. Once no kext is needed, you can restore full security in Startup Security Utility (recoveryOS).
mac.kb.docks.title: Crashes linked to docks, hubs and USB-C / Thunderbolt accessories
mac.kb.docks.symptoms: Panics, freezes or displays going black when an accessory is plugged in, unplugged, or when the Mac wakes. The report may mention USB or Thunderbolt.
mac.kb.docks.cause: Docks and hubs combine displays, network, audio and storage behind one cable; a faulty cable, power supply or dock firmware can disturb the whole bus.
mac.kb.docks.fix: Test without the dock for a few days. Use the cable and power supply that came with the dock, update its firmware, and connect displays directly when possible. Reconnect devices one at a time to find the faulty one.
mac.kb.low_disk.title: Slowdowns and crashes when the startup disk is almost full
mac.kb.low_disk.symptoms: Spinning pointer, apps closing, "Your system has run out of application memory", updates that fail to install.
mac.kb.low_disk.cause: macOS uses free disk space for swap (virtual memory), caches and updates. Below about 10 % free, memory pressure rises and the system becomes unstable.
mac.kb.low_disk.fix: Open System Settings › General › Storage and remove what you no longer need (large files, old backups of iPhone / iPad, unused apps, simulators and developer caches). Keep at least 10 % of the disk free.
mac.kb.memory.title: Apps quit on their own: macOS runs out of memory
mac.kb.memory.symptoms: Apps or browser tabs close or reload, "JetsamEvent" reports, the Memory Pressure graph turns yellow or red in Activity Monitor.
mac.kb.memory.cause: Too many apps or tabs open for the installed memory, a single app leaking memory, or too little free disk space for swap.
mac.kb.memory.fix: In Activity Monitor › Memory, sort by memory to find the heaviest app and restart it. Close unused tabs and virtual machines, keep disk space free, and restart the Mac now and then.
mac.kb.apps_update.title: An app crashes after a macOS update
mac.kb.apps_update.symptoms: The same app quits at launch or on the same action, with a crash report each time, since a macOS update.
mac.kb.apps_update.cause: The app, one of its plug-ins or its cached data are not compatible with the new macOS version yet.
mac.kb.apps_update.fix: Update the app (App Store or the vendor's site). Remove or update its plug-ins. If it keeps crashing, quit it, move its preferences out of ~/Library/Preferences, or reinstall it.
mac.kb.gpu.title: Graphics glitches and GPU panics
mac.kb.gpu.symptoms: Flickering, black screens, artefacts, or panics whose report mentions the GPU (AGX).
mac.kb.gpu.cause: A graphics driver problem, triggered by an external display, an adapter, a game or a 3D / video app; more rarely a hardware fault.
mac.kb.gpu.fix: Update macOS and the app involved. Test without external displays and adapters. If it also happens with Apple apps only and nothing connected, run Apple Diagnostics and contact Apple support.
mac.kb.ssd.title: Storage errors and disk-related panics
mac.kb.ssd.symptoms: Files that cannot be read, disk errors in Disk Utility, panics mentioning the SSD controller, a SMART status other than "Verified".
mac.kb.ssd.cause: File-system damage after a crash or a forced shutdown, an external drive or cable fault, or more rarely a failing internal SSD.
mac.kb.ssd.fix: Back up first. Run First Aid in Disk Utility on the disk and its volumes. For external drives, change the cable and port. A failing internal SSD on Apple Silicon needs Apple support.
mac.kb.heat.title: Overheating and fans at full speed
mac.kb.heat.symptoms: The Mac is hot, the fans run loud, performance drops; sometimes the Mac shuts down on its own.
mac.kb.heat.cause: A process stuck using the processor, blocked vents (bed, cushion, case), a hot room, or a heavy workload over a long time.
mac.kb.heat.fix: In Activity Monitor › CPU, quit the process that uses the most. Use the Mac on a hard, flat surface with clear vents. Keep macOS up to date.
mac.kb.battery.title: MacBook shuts down suddenly on battery
mac.kb.battery.symptoms: The MacBook turns off while the battery still shows charge left, especially under load or in the cold.
mac.kb.battery.cause: A worn battery can no longer deliver peak power: the voltage drops and the Mac shuts down to protect itself.
mac.kb.battery.fix: Check the battery condition and maximum capacity in System Settings › Battery. Below 80 %, or if macOS recommends service, have the battery replaced.
mac.kb.safe_mode.title: Find the cause with safe mode and Apple Diagnostics
mac.kb.safe_mode.symptoms: Crashes or freezes with no clear pattern, at startup or soon after login.
mac.kb.safe_mode.cause: A login item, a third-party extension or damaged caches load at startup; or a hardware fault.
mac.kb.safe_mode.fix: Safe mode on Apple Silicon: shut down, hold the power button until the startup options appear, select the startup disk, hold Shift and click "Continue in Safe Mode". If the problem disappears, remove login items one by one. For hardware, run Apple Diagnostics: shut down, hold the power button, then press Command-D.
mac.kb.panic_reports.title: Read a kernel panic report
mac.kb.panic_reports.symptoms: After a restart, macOS shows "Your computer restarted because of a problem" and offers to send a report.
mac.kb.panic_reports.cause: macOS writes each panic to /Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports (.panic files). The useful lines are the panic message, the panicked task and "Kernel Extensions in backtrace".
mac.kb.panic_reports.fix: Dump Finder reads these files for you (Crashes tab). In Console, Crash Reports shows them too. A non-Apple bundle id in the backtrace points to the software to update or remove; the same message repeating points to one cause.

health.bios_memory_pcie_link_ssd_softwar: Chip, memory, SSD, battery, screens and third-party extensions — what macOS reports about this Mac.
hosting.the_windows_utilities_that_help_: The macOS utilities that help diagnose, and the full report to share.
onboarding.when_windows_crashes_it_leave: When macOS crashes it leaves traces: kernel panic reports and .ips crash reports. Dump Finder reads them for you and puts them in plain words.
onboarding.30_days_of_logs_dmp_files: 90 days of reports, kernel extensions, SSD, battery: everything is read-only. Nothing changes on your Mac.
onboarding.home_shows_a_30_day_stability: Home shows a 30-day stability score and the actions that help. Every crash has its own page in Crashes, with the explanation and the report file.
onboarding.tip_the_stability_test_tab_ch: Tip: the "Extensions" tab lists the third-party kernel and system extensions, the usual suspects of a kernel panic.
mac.hw.os_ok: This macOS version still receives security updates. On a Mac, firmware updates come with macOS updates: there is no BIOS to update separately.
mac.hw.chip_detail: Apple Silicon puts the processor, graphics and memory on one chip: there is no memory profile, overclocking or graphics driver to set up. Graphics updates come with macOS.
mac.hw.memory_ok: Memory pressure is low: apps have room to run.
mac.hw.memory_warn: macOS is short of memory ({0} % free, {1:0.#} GB of swap). It compresses memory and writes to the SSD, which slows the Mac down and can close apps.
mac.hw.memory_guide_steps:
1. Open Activity Monitor › Memory and sort by Memory.
2. Quit the apps or browser tabs that use the most.
3. Restart the Mac if memory pressure stays yellow or red.
mac.hw.ssd_ok: SMART status verified: the drive reports no fault.
mac.hw.battery_ok: The battery holds its charge normally.
mac.hw.thermal_ok: macOS reports no thermal or performance warning right now.
mac.hw.thermal_warn: macOS is slowing the chip down to cool it. Heavy apps run slower, and the fans may be loud.
mac.hw.thermal_advice: Make sure the vents are clear and the Mac is not on a soft surface. Look in Activity Monitor › CPU for an app using the processor in the background.
mac.hw.displays_detail: Flickering, black screens or a WindowServer freeze after plugging in a screen often come from the cable, the adapter or the dock: try a direct connection.
mac.hw.devices_title: one: {0} USB / Thunderbolt device | other: {0} USB / Thunderbolt devices
mac.hw.devices_detail: Docks, hubs and adapters are a common cause of kernel panics and wake-up problems. If a crash happens when a device is plugged in or the Mac wakes up, unplug it to compare.
mac.hw.errors_value: one: {0} reading failed | other: {0} readings failed
mac.cf.sip_ok: SIP protects system files from being changed, including by installers and kernel extensions.
mac.cf.gk_ok: Gatekeeper checks that the apps you open are signed by an identified developer and checked by Apple.
mac.cf.kext_none: No third-party kernel extension: the most common cause of kernel panics is ruled out.
mac.cf.kext_some: Kernel extensions run inside the macOS kernel: a fault in one of them causes a kernel panic. Apple is replacing them with system extensions, which run outside the kernel.
mac.cf.sysext_detail: Network filters, VPNs, antivirus and drivers in the new format. They run outside the kernel, but a faulty network or security filter can still freeze the Mac or cut the connection.
mac.cf.apps_ok: No app crashed {0} times or more in the last {1} days.
mac.cf.apps_some: These apps crashed several times. An update or a reinstall usually fixes it; if the crashes started after a macOS update, check the developer's site.
mac.cf.uptime_ok: A regular restart applies pending updates and clears memory leaks.
mac.ext.summary: {0} third-party extensions · {1} not loaded · {2} implicated in a crash.
mac.ext.none_body: Only Apple's own extensions are loaded: nothing to check here.
